Rabati Castle (Akhaltsikhe)

A restored fortress-town in the heart of Akhaltsikhe where a mosque, a church and a synagogue share one courtyard.

Time needed
2 h
From Tbilisi
205 km · 3:20
Road
Paved
Car needed
Economy class
Season
All year
Entry
~20 ₾ (ზედა ეზო)

Rabati is the historic core of Akhaltsikhe: a walled town on a hill that served for centuries as the seat of the Jaqeli princes and later as the centre of Ottoman administration in the region. The name comes from an Arabic word for a fortified quarter.

The complex was extensively rebuilt in 2011-2012, and that restoration is still argued about. Some of what you walk past is genuinely old, some is modern reconstruction in pale stone with new gardens and terraces. Either way, Rabati remains a rare place in Georgia where the religious layering of Meskheti sits in one enclosure — a mosque with its madrasa, an Orthodox church, a synagogue building and part of the princely palace.

The site splits into two zones:

  • the lower free zone — lanes, cafes, souvenir shops, tourist information
  • the upper ticketed zone — the citadel, the mosque, the history museum and access to the ramparts

From the upper walls you see the whole town and the ridges of Meskheti. The museum inside covers regional archaeology and the Jaqeli period, and is worth the extra twenty minutes.

Practical advice

Rabati is the natural break on a Vardzia trip, and it works better on the way back, when you are no longer racing the clock at the cave city. Two hours covers it comfortably. Park at the lot by the lower entrance. In summer the stone courtyards get genuinely hot and shade is scarce; in the evening the lighting makes for good photographs. Cafes, toilets and ATMs are in the lower zone, with shops and fuel in the town itself.

How to get there from Tbilisi

From Tbilisi take the E60 to Khashuri, then head south to Borjomi and continue through the narrow rocky stretch of the Mtkvari valley to Akhaltsikhe — roughly three and a half hours in total. The road is paved and in good condition throughout, though the Borjomi-Akhaltsikhe section is narrow and winding, and ices over in winter. Fuel and ATMs are available in both Borjomi and Akhaltsikhe. An economy car is entirely sufficient; a crossover simply rides the winter road more comfortably.
